answer: The paper's P/D disaggregation latency model holds qualitatively but breaks down quantitatively in BLIS, and we can trace the breakdown to three precise mechanisms. (1) QUALITATIVE: The paper's predictions are fully confirmed — AD always has lower ITL than AL (max diff 1.685ms at rate=140), AD always has higher TTFT than AL (pipeline overhead 4-16ms), and AD wins on E2E at all tested rates. (2) QUANTITATIVE ITL FORMULA: ITL = alpha/(1-rho) fits within 0.5% for rho < 0.10 (rates 1-20), but overpredicts by 6% at rho=0.29 (rate=60), 28% at rho=0.48 (rate=100), and 122% at rho=0.73 (rate=150). The paper predicts instability at lambda_max=207 req/s, but BLIS runs stably at 150 req/s with ITL=19.9ms vs the predicted 44.2ms. (3) BREAKDOWN MECHANISM: The paper's formula derives steady-state batch size B_ss via Little's law, requiring B_ss = lambda*(n_c+o)*T_iter. At rate=150, B_ss=424 per instance — but only 150 requests arrive, so the batch reaches at most 102 (24% of steady state). The finite 300-request horizon prevents the self-reinforcing feedback loop that drives the 1/(1-rho) blowup. (4) CORRECTED MODEL: A transient batch-dynamics simulation that tracks discrete request lifecycles (prefill/decode), computes batch-size-weighted ITL (matching BLIS's AllITLs metric), and uses deterministic arrivals (matching BLIS's least-loaded routing) reproduces BLIS within 0.05% RMSE across ALL rates 1-150 for both AL and AD. The three key corrections over the paper's formula: (a) finite-horizon batch dynamics instead of Little's law steady state, (b) batch-size-weighted ITL instead of simple step-time average (7% bias at high rates), (c) BLIS's least-loaded routing produces effectively deterministic per-instance arrivals, not Poisson.
